title: Methodus nova et facilis calculum variationum tractandi

deep.reconstruction:
Context: in §§49–53 of E420, Euler sorts integral functionals ∫Z dx, with Z = Z(x,y,p,q), p = y', q = y'', into 'classes' according to the differential order of the resulting Euler–Lagrange equation. That order fixes how many boundary data the problem needs.

Class II (§50, previous page): Z = Z(x,y,p) with Z_pp ≠ 0. This gives a 2nd-order equation N − dP/dx = 0 and two endpoint conditions.

§51 (this page) adds to Class II the Lagrangians that are linear in q: Z = 𝔷(x,y,p)·q.
- Write d𝔷 = 𝔐dx + 𝔑dy + 𝔓dp. Then M = 𝔐q, N = 𝔑q, P = 𝔓q and Q = 𝔷.
- The general 4th-order equation 0 = N − dP/dx + d²Q/dx² is written as 0 = N − (1/dx)·d(P − dQ/dx).
- Since dQ/dx = d𝔷/dx = 𝔐 + 𝔑p + 𝔓q, the q-terms cancel: P − dQ/dx = −𝔐 − 𝔑p.
- The equation therefore becomes 0 = 𝔑q + d(𝔐 + 𝔑p)/dx = 2𝔑q + d𝔐/dx + p·d𝔑/dx. Since 𝔐 and 𝔑 depend only on x, y, p, this is of 2nd order only.

Generalisation: for ∫(Z + 𝔷q)dx with Z, 𝔷 functions of x, y, p, the equation is 0 = N − dP/dx + 2𝔑q + d𝔐/dx + p·d𝔑/dx. Equivalently, 0 = N dx − dP + 2𝔑 dp + d𝔐 + p d𝔑, again of 2nd order.

§52 starts Class III: Q = Z_q itself contains q, the equation is of 4th order, and four boundary data are needed (endpoints and endpoint tangents). This leads to the elastica example of §53.

Modern reading of §51: if F_p = 𝔷, then 𝔷q = dF/dx − F_x − F_y·p. So the q-linear Lagrangian differs from a first-order Lagrangian by a total derivative, i.e. a null Lagrangian. That is why the order drops. Euler shows the drop by direct cancellation and does not state this total-derivative mechanism.
errors: No mathematical errors. Euler's equation agrees with the equation obtained from the equivalent first-order Lagrangian −F_x − F_y·p, where F_p = 𝔷.

Minor gap: Euler asserts the equation is genuinely of 2nd order. The coefficient of q is 𝔷_xp + p·𝔷_yp + 2𝔷_y, which can vanish. If 𝔷 = 𝔷(p), the whole equation vanishes identically (∫𝔷(p)q dx = ∫d G(p) is a pure boundary term). Euler does not remark on such further degenerations.

ideas.what: A Lagrangian linear in the highest derivative y'' yields an Euler–Lagrange equation of order 2 rather than 4.
ideas.modern_name: Degenerate higher-order Lagrangians; reduction modulo total derivatives (null Lagrangians)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Folklore of the classical calculus of variations; the systematic theory is later (Ostrogradsky 1850 for higher-order mechanics; 20th-century work on null Lagrangians and the variational bicomplex).
ideas.where_published: Possibly anticipated in E65 (Methodus inveniendi, 1744), ch. on formulas involving second derivatives; unsure.

ideas.what: Classification of variational problems by the differential order of the Euler equation and the matching number of boundary conditions.
ideas.modern_name: Order of Euler–Lagrange equations and natural boundary-value counting

deep.surprise_reason: A correct, routine order-reduction computation for q-linear Lagrangians. The underlying total-derivative fact is elementary and well known; Euler does not even make the null-Lagrangian interpretation explicit.
transcription_corrections: Transcription is accurate. The Fraktur symbols 𝔷, 𝔐, 𝔑, 𝔓 are correctly rendered; the 'Z' in 'Z = 𝔷q' on the first line is the italic/roman Z of the integrand.
